posts.title: What a wet week does to an entrance
posts.excerpt: A wet week loads the mat inside the door with rain and grit, and the round has a simple answer: an extra swap, then the planned one in week four.
posts.content:
A wet week shows itself first on the pavement. Shoe-prints hold in the water. Rain beads on the glass. The street is still dark when the round starts at 06:30, and the entrance is the only part of the building that has already done a day’s work. Everything the street is carrying stops, or fails to stop, at that sill.

Inside the door the mat is the stop. It is charcoal, laid just inside the glass, on the dry side of the line. People cross it without looking. Water comes off their shoes. Grit comes with the water. By the second wet morning the pile at the edge is darker than it was on install day. That is the mat doing what it was put there to do. It is also the reason a four-week stretch can feel short when the weather turns.

On an ordinary round nobody comes back in week two or week three. The mat stays down. The fitter is on other doorways, Monday to Saturday, and the next planned visit is the swap in week four. A wet week is the exception we already price. If the mat is loaded before that swap, the site can book an extra swap visit at €12. The fitter rolls the wet mat out, lays a fresh one in the same place, and puts the used mat in the van. The four-week round does not restart unless you ask for something else. Week four still comes.

Offices notice it in the lobby. Staff arrive together, shoes still wet from the walk between the street and the glass. Northgate Offices keeps a mat inside those doors for that reason. Daniel Mensah, facilities, takes the early install so the mat is already down. A wet week does not change his doorway. It only fills the pile sooner. An extra swap is a phone call to the desk, not a different kind of hire.

The used mat does not stay in the lobby to dry. It goes to the depot at Unit 4, Canal Yard, Easton. Liesel Brandt washes it and inspects it in the room where mats hang on rails. The entrance never becomes a washroom. Priya Raman and Jonah Weiss carry the roll. The install they did, weeks earlier, took about 20 minutes: measure the doorway, unroll the mat, leave it. The extra swap is the same kind of visit, shorter in intention. Lift, lay, go.

Shops feel the wet week at the moment they open. The pavement outside a bakery door holds the night’s rain, and the first customers bring it in on their shoes. Hearth & Crumb is one of those doors. Sofia Marin, the owner, has a mat just inside. She can ask for the €12 visit when the week is wet. She is not asked to hose the mat or to hang it in the kitchen. Care of the mat sits with the depot. Care of the doorway, for her, is having a dry pile in place when the door unlocks.

A clinic entrance has a quieter version of the same morning. Patients step from wet pavement onto the mat and then into a calm room. Easton Dental, where Dr. Lena Kowalski has a mat at the door, is that kind of threshold. A wet week does not ask the reception staff to do anything to the mat. If it needs to go early, the round takes it. If it can wait, it waits for week four.

The trial month is built for one site and one cycle of this. One 85 × 150 cm mat, the install, and one swap, at €19. After that the standard price is €24 every four weeks. A larger door uses a larger mat at its own price. None of those prices changes because the week was wet. The only added figure is the extra swap at €12, and only if you book it. There is no contract. When the weather pattern is not what you want to keep paying for, you resize or you stop, and stopping carries no fee.

What a wet week does, then, is ordinary. It prints the street on the pile. It asks, once, whether the planned swap is soon enough. If it is, the mat stays and week four proceeds. If it is not, a fitter comes at the start of the day, as on any other install morning, and the entrance has a fresh mat before the first customer. The rest of the building can stay as it was.
